narrative:
The 2025 Baltimore Orioles were a team that never quite found its footing, finishing 75-87 and missing the playoffs in what amounted to a painful step backward from the organization's recent rise. The offense generated a respectable 191 home runs but an anemic .699 OPS told the real story — too many empty at-bats, too little consistency. A pitching staff that allowed 788 runs and posted a 4.60 ERA couldn't compensate, and a bullpen that repeatedly imploded in critical moments became the defining wound of the season.

The early going in May offered both promise and heartbreak in equal measure. Félix Bautista, returning from injury, struggled to recapture his dominance and became a symbol of the team's fragility in close games. His back-to-back blown saves in mid-to-late May were devastating, giving away wins Baltimore desperately needed. Yet amid the chaos, Cedric Mullins delivered a grand slam that briefly lit up Camden Yards, and Ryan O'Hearn provided a three-run blast that kept faint playoff hopes alive. The Orioles were a team of moments — brilliant flashes surrounded by structural collapse.

The summer months told a story of Gunnar Henderson carrying a franchise on his back. Three massive home runs between late June and early August gave Baltimore its only sustained stretches of competitive baseball, and his three-run shot on August 2nd — the single highest-leverage positive play of the season — was the kind of swing that briefly made fans believe. But Keegan Akin's chronic late-game meltdowns in August, including two crushing home runs allowed that together cost the team nearly 1.1 WPA, erased those moments as quickly as Henderson created them.

The September stretch offered a bittersweet coda. Young players like Samuel Basallo, Coby Mayo, Dylan Beavers, and Jackson Holliday flashed genuine upside, and Emmanuel Rivera's improbable walk-off single on September 6th — the most impactful positive play of the entire season — gave a glimpse of what this group might become. Colton Cowser's 15th home run in mid-September and Mayo's late-season blast showed a youth movement with real teeth. But the damage was already done. The 2025 Orioles will be remembered not as a team that failed, but as one caught between eras — veterans fading, youngsters not yet ready, and a bullpen that bridged the gap in entirely the wrong direction.

chapters.title: Shaky Starts and May Mayhem
chapters.description: A turbulent May defined by bullpen collapses and fleeting offensive sparks set an ominous tone for Baltimore's season.

chapters.title: Flickers of Fight
chapters.description: Late May and early June produced a pair of clutch multi-run hits that briefly ignited hope and steadied a listing ship.

chapters.title: Henderson's One-Man Show
chapters.description: Gunnar Henderson emerged as the undisputed heart of the Orioles through June and July, delivering back-to-back go-ahead home runs while the rest of the roster sputtered.

chapters.title: August Unraveling
chapters.description: Three brutal bullpen implosions in August — headlined by Keegan Akin's repeated late-game disasters — buried Baltimore's playoff chances for good.

chapters.title: Youth Rising from the Rubble
chapters.description: September brought a silver lining as Basallo, Mayo, Beavers, and Holliday delivered meaningful moments that hinted at a brighter future even as the season's fate was sealed.
